subtopics.name: Points, vectors & distances
subtopics.summary: Representing points and vectors with integer coordinates, computing Euclidean and squared distances, dot products and basic vector arithmetic. Appears in easy problems about distances, circles around the origin and moving on the plane; recognise it whenever coordinates are given and comparisons of lengths are needed.
learn: Store points as pair<long long,long long> or a small struct with +, -, scalar * operators (or std::complex as in CPH 29.1)
Compare distances using squared lengths (dx*dx+dy*dy) to stay in exact integer arithmetic; take sqrt only for the final output
Dot product a.x*b.x+a.y*b.y: zero means perpendicular, sign tells acute/obtuse angle
Watch overflow: coordinates up to 1e9 give squared distances up to ~8e18, use long long (or __int128)
Print floating answers with enough digits (setprecision(10)) and use long double when precision matters
Translate the problem so one point is the origin to simplify formulas
Vector identities: ABCD is a parallelogram iff the diagonals share a midpoint (A+C = B+D); a polygon is centrally symmetric iff p_i + p_{i+n/2} is constant
The same tools work in 3D: squared distances and dot products identify cubes, right angles and equal edges

subtopics.name: Rectangle geometry
subtopics.summary: Axis-aligned rectangles: area, intersection, union of two or three rectangles and coverage checks. Very common in Div 3/4 and early Div 2 problems; recognise it when shapes are given by lower-left and upper-right corners.
learn: Intersection of [x1,x2]x[y1,y2] and [x3,x4]x[y3,y4] is [max(x1,x3),min(x2,x4)] x [max(y1,y3),min(y2,y4)], empty if any side is negative
Area of union of two rectangles = A + B - intersection (inclusion-exclusion)
To test if a rectangle is fully covered, subtract covered parts and check what remains
Prefix/suffix intersections let you drop one rectangle in O(1) (intersection of all but one)
Compress coordinates when many rectangles are involved, then sweep or use 2D difference arrays

subtopics.name: Manhattan & Chebyshev distance
subtopics.summary: Manhattan distance |dx|+|dy| separates into coordinates and becomes Chebyshev distance after rotating by 45 degrees (u=x+y, v=x-y). Recognise it in grid-walking problems, sums of pairwise distances and farthest-pair queries.
learn: Sum of |xi-xj| over all pairs: sort and use prefix sums, independently for x and y
Rotation trick: |dx|+|dy| = max(|du|,|dv|) with u=x+y, v=x-y; max Manhattan distance = max over the four sign combinations
Chebyshev distance max(|dx|,|dy|) is king moves on a grid; convert back with the inverse rotation
Manhattan circles are diamonds; diamonds become axis-aligned squares after rotation
Points with equal Manhattan and Euclidean distance share x or y (count with maps and subtract duplicates)
Terms like max(0, p - |x - j|) are tents; the rotation (j+x, j-x) turns "is every point covered" into two prefix-max checks
Short Manhattan tours: sort points in vertical strips of width ~sqrt(C), alternating direction (Mo-style ordering)

subtopics.name: Cross product & orientation
subtopics.summary: The cross product a.x*b.y-a.y*b.x gives twice the signed area of a triangle and tells whether a turn is left, right or collinear. It is the core primitive of almost all computational geometry; recognise it whenever you must decide on which side of a line a point lies.
learn: cross(b-a, c-a) > 0: counter-clockwise (left turn), < 0: clockwise, = 0: collinear
Keep everything in integers (long long / __int128) so orientation tests are exact
|cross| / 2 is the triangle area; non-degenerate triangle iff cross != 0
Collinearity of many points: fix one point and normalise direction vectors (divide by gcd, fix sign) to group them
Dot product decides angle type; cross product decides side - combine them to sort or classify
Interactive problems may ask only for orientation signs: build convex order from sign queries

subtopics.name: Lines: representation & intersection
subtopics.summary: Representing lines as ax+by=c or point+direction, normalising them for hashing, checking parallelism and computing intersection points. Recognise it in counting problems about lines through pairs of points or intersection counts.
learn: Line through p,q: a=q.y-p.y, b=p.x-q.x, c=a*p.x+b*p.y; normalise (divide by gcd, make first non-zero positive) to store in a set/map
Two lines are parallel iff a1*b2-a2*b1=0; intersection uses Cramer's rule with that determinant
Number of intersecting pairs = total pairs minus pairs within each parallel class
Normalised direction vectors (dx/g, dy/g) identify slopes exactly without floating point
Use exact rational comparisons (cross-multiplication) instead of comparing slopes as doubles
Distance from point P to line AB = |cross(B-A, P-A)| / |B-A|; it bounds how far a convex vertex can move before the polygon stops being convex

subtopics.name: Segment intersection
subtopics.summary: Deciding whether two segments intersect using orientation tests, including collinear-overlap edge cases, and computing the intersection point. Recognise it when segments, fences, chords or paths must not cross.
learn: Proper intersection: orientations of (a,b,c) and (a,b,d) differ AND orientations of (c,d,a) and (c,d,b) differ
Collinear case: all four orientations are zero, then check overlap of bounding boxes/projections
Point on segment: cross = 0 and the point lies within the bounding box
Chords of a circle intersect iff their endpoints interleave around the circle
Lattice points on a segment: gcd(|dx|,|dy|)+1 (useful for counting covered integer points)
Test edge cases: shared endpoints, zero-length segments, vertical segments

subtopics.name: Polygon area & point in polygon
subtopics.summary: Shoelace formula for the area of a simple polygon and ray casting / winding tests for point-in-polygon, plus O(log n) point-in-convex-polygon by binary search. Recognise it whenever a polygon is given as a vertex list.
learn: Shoelace: 2*Area = |sum cross(p_i, p_{i+1})|; keep twice the area as an integer
Sign of the sum gives orientation (CCW positive)
Ray casting: count crossings of a horizontal ray; handle points on the boundary separately
Convex polygon: binary search the fan of triangles from vertex 0 for O(log n) queries
Triangulation and area-based DP: split polygon by diagonals, check diagonal validity with cross products
Area of triangle/quadrilateral maximisation: fix a diagonal, take best point on each side
Counting triangles of polygon vertices that contain a point: count the complement (triangles lying in a half-plane through the point) with two pointers

resources.title: Check if point belongs to the convex polygon

subtopics.name: Pick's theorem & lattice points
subtopics.summary: Pick's theorem A = i + b/2 - 1 relates area, interior and boundary lattice points of a lattice polygon; boundary points on an edge are gcd(|dx|,|dy|). Recognise it when counting integer points inside/on a polygon or constructing lattice triangles of given area.
learn: Boundary points b = sum over edges gcd(|dx|,|dy|)
Interior points i = A - b/2 + 1 with A from the shoelace formula (use 2A to stay integer)
Lattice triangle area is always a multiple of 1/2: 2A must be an integer, which gives feasibility conditions
Lattice points inside a circle/annulus: loop over x and compute the y-range with integer sqrt
Lattice points under a line: floor-sum style counting (see number theory area)
Parity tricks: with Pick, the parity of interior points depends only on coordinates mod 4 and gcds mod 4, so classify points into residue classes and count

subtopics.name: Floating point, circles & numeric geometry
subtopics.summary: Problems involving circles, angles, trigonometry and continuous optimisation where answers are real numbers. Recognise them from "absolute or relative error 1e-6" outputs; they often combine geometry with binary or ternary search on the answer.
learn: Use long double, compare with an epsilon, and avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers
acos/asin need arguments clamped to [-1,1]
Circle-circle and circle-line intersections: derive with distances and the cosine rule
Distance from point to segment: project with the dot product, clamp to the segment
Tangent circles: centres of touching circles of radii r1,r2 are r1+r2 apart; solve for the unknown coordinate with Pythagoras
Binary search the answer (radius, time) when a monotone feasibility check exists; ternary search for unimodal functions
Regular polygons: central angle 2*pi/n; inscribed/circumscribed radius formulas

subtopics.name: Angular (polar) sort
subtopics.summary: Sorting vectors by angle around a point using half-plane classification plus cross product, avoiding atan2 precision issues. Recognise it when you need consecutive directions, angle gaps, rotating sweeps or counting triangles/configurations around a pivot.
learn: Split vectors into upper half (y>0 or y=0,x>0) and lower half, then compare by cross product inside each half
atan2 with long double works for moderate coordinates but can fail for nearly parallel vectors
Minimum angle between vectors: sort and check adjacent pairs including the wrap-around
Angular sweep around each point gives O(n^2 log n) algorithms for counting triangles/quadrilaterals
Normalised directions (gcd) group identical rays exactly

subtopics.name: Convex hull
subtopics.summary: Computing the convex hull of a point set with Andrew's monotone chain (or Graham scan) in O(n log n), and using hull properties for extreme-point queries. Recognise it when only the "outer" points matter, when maximising a linear function or when lower/upper envelopes of prefix sums appear.
learn: Monotone chain: sort by (x,y), build lower and upper hulls with a stack popping non-left turns
Decide whether collinear points on edges are kept (<= vs < in the pop condition)
Lower hull of points (i, prefix_i) gives optimal averages/greedy merges (Water Balance pattern)
Transform the problem (e.g. y -> y - x^2) to turn parabolas into lines and use the upper hull
Farthest pair / largest triangle use the hull plus rotating calipers
Point-in-convex-polygon and tangents by binary search on the hull

subtopics.name: Sweep line in geometry
subtopics.summary: Process events (segment endpoints, rectangle edges) sorted by x while maintaining an active set ordered by y in a data structure. Recognise it when counting intersections of horizontal/vertical segments, union area/perimeter of rectangles or covered points.
learn: Events: (x, type, data); choose the tie-break order of start/end events carefully
Horizontal/vertical segment intersections: add/remove horizontals at endpoints, query a Fenwick tree for verticals
Union area of rectangles: segment tree over compressed y storing cover count and covered length
Pieces of a square cut by segments = 1 + segments spanning full side + intersections (Euler formula)
Use coordinate compression and 64-bit counts

resources.title: Search for a pair of intersecting segments

subtopics.name: Closest pair of points
subtopics.summary: Find the two closest points in O(n log n) by sweeping with a set ordered by y (CPH) or by divide and conquer on x. Recognise it when minimising a distance-like expression over pairs, sometimes after rewriting it as a point distance (e.g. prefix sums).
learn: Sweep: keep points with x within d of the current point in a set ordered by y; only O(1) candidates per point
Divide and conquer: split by median x, merge strips sorted by y, check next ~7 points
Rewrite pair expressions like (i-j)^2 + (pre_i - pre_j)^2 as squared distance between (i, pre_i) points
Keep distances squared in long long; randomised grid hashing is an alternative expected O(n) method

resources.title: Finding the nearest pair of points

subtopics.name: Minkowski sum, half-planes & rotating calipers
subtopics.summary: Advanced convex geometry: Minkowski sum of convex polygons by merging edges in angular order, half-plane intersection with a deque, and rotating calipers for diameters/widths. Rare below 2400 but standard in harder geometry problems.
learn: Minkowski sum of convex polygons: start at the lowest point of each and merge edge vectors by polar angle; result has <= n+m vertices
Number of distinct edge directions = number of vertices of a Minkowski sum (Geometers Anonymous)
Half-plane intersection: sort by angle, maintain a deque, pop while the last intersection is outside
Rotating calipers: two pointers on the hull for diameter, width, max-area triangle
Point in Minkowski sum = can be represented as a sum of points from each polygon

subtopics.name: Good RNG & hashing custom keys
subtopics.summary: Use mt19937 seeded by time instead of rand(), and protect unordered_map / hashing against anti-hash tests with a randomised custom hash (splitmix64). Turn mathematical objects into canonical keys (reduced fractions, transformed values) so they can be counted in a hash map. Matters on Codeforces because open hacking targets predictable hashes.
learn: mt19937_64 rng(chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count()); uniform_int_distribution for ranges; shuffle(v.begin(), v.end(), rng)
rand() has RAND_MAX 32767 on some judges and is predictable
unordered_map can be blown up to O(n) per operation by crafted tests; use a splitmix64 hash with a random offset, or map
Polynomial hashing: random base, mod 2^61-1 or two moduli to avoid anti-hash tests
Use canonical keys (normalised fractions with sign fixed, prime-signature vectors) when hashing mathematical objects
Algebraic rewriting into a key: (a+b)(a^2+b^2) = k  <=>  a^4 - k*a = b^4 - k*b (mod p) after multiplying by (a-b)

resources.title: Don't use rand(): a guide to random number generators in C++
Blowing up unordered_map, and how to stop getting hacked on it

subtopics.name: Random input, expected behaviour & birthday paradox
subtopics.summary: Some problems promise random tests or contain a random process; then the answer has a provable typical shape (first 1 bit appears early, few prefix maxima, small depth) or a pigeonhole/birthday argument bounds the brute force. Recognise statements that say "tests are generated randomly", or when values are bounded so a collision must appear quickly.
learn: Random binary string: the first 1 and the first 0 after it appear within O(log n) positions with high probability, so "try only a few shifts" is enough
Random permutations: expected number of prefix maxima is O(log n); a random swap changes inversion parity, so parity identifies the number of swaps
Birthday/pigeonhole: if pair sums lie in [1, 2V], among more than 2V pairs two must collide, so brute force over pairs stops after O(V) steps
Randomised algorithms with expected guarantees: random shuffle before incremental algorithms (min enclosing circle), random pivot in quicksort/quickselect
Random binary trees and random walks have O(log n) / O(sqrt n) typical sizes; exploit them only when the statement guarantees randomness
Always analyse failure probability across all tests (union bound) before relying on luck

subtopics.name: Random sampling (frequent elements, Monte Carlo)
subtopics.summary: Monte Carlo sampling: if the answer is determined by an element that occupies at least a 1/k fraction of the data (majority, half of the array, every friend likes the currency), pick random elements and verify each candidate. Recognise "at least half / more than a third / at least n/2 elements" conditions where a deterministic solution looks much harder.
learn: If an element appears in >= 1/k of positions, ~20-30*k random picks find it with failure probability (1-1/k)^tries
Range majority: sample random positions in [l, r] and count occurrences with binary search on per-value position lists
Ghd / gcd of at least half: a random element is in the optimal half with probability 1/2; test all its divisors
Kuroni-style: with cost <= n, at least half of the elements change by <= 1, so try prime factors of a_i - 1, a_i, a_i + 1 for random i
Love-Hate: fix a random person in the answer and run SOS DP over the <= 15 currencies they like
Deterministic alternatives exist (Boyer-Moore voting on a segment tree, persistent tree); choose by implementation time

subtopics.name: Randomization in interactive problems
subtopics.summary: Interactive problems with a query limit often need randomness: random probes to estimate an unknown size, random pivots to sort with comparison-like queries, or random choices to defeat an adaptive-looking interactor. Recognise a query budget like 2n, 40n or 60n where the deterministic worst case is too slow but the expected cost fits.
learn: Sample random positions to land close to the target, then finish with a deterministic walk or binary search
Random pivots (quicksort-style) give expected O(n log n) queries for sorting/reconstruction problems
Random large jumps estimate an unknown cycle length (max seen label), then baby-step giant-step finishes it
If the interactor answers randomly, repeat queries and use the answers that cannot both be wrong
Shrink a candidate region by querying a random point inside it: expected O(log n) rounds
Use a fixed-seed-free RNG (time-seeded mt19937) so hacks cannot target your choices

subtopics.name: Bitset optimisation (graphs, matrices, sets)
subtopics.summary: std::bitset packs booleans into 64-bit words so AND/OR/XOR/shift/popcount run n/64 times faster. Recognise it when an O(n^2) or O(n^3) boolean computation is just slightly too slow (n around 1e4-5e4).
learn: bitset<N> needs a compile-time N; use the maximum constraint
count(), _Find_first(), _Find_next(i) iterate set bits quickly
Common uses: popcount of intersections (common neighbours, counting corner rectangles), reachability in DAGs (reach[v] |= reach[u])
Complexity becomes O(n^2 / w) or O(n^3 / w) with w = 64
Process DAG reachability in reverse topological order; for memory, process vertices in blocks
Precompute per-element bitsets and answer queries with XOR/AND + count
Pattern matching with wildcards/updates: keep one bitset of positions per letter, AND shifted letter bitsets (shift-and); O(n*m/64)
Pairs/triangles: for each point keep a bitset of points farther than d and test pairs with (a & b).any() while scanning edges in decreasing length

subtopics.name: Divide & conquer basics
subtopics.summary: Solve a problem by splitting the input into halves (or around the minimum/maximum), solving recursively and combining. Recognise it when the structure is self-similar (strings of length 2^k, building a tree from a max, splitting a range at its minimum).
learn: Write solve(l, r) and identify the combine step and the base case
Split at the maximum/minimum to build Cartesian-tree-like recursions
Recursion depth: halving gives O(log n); splitting at extremes can be O(n), consider an explicit stack
Complexity via the master theorem: T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) = O(n log n)
Enumerate all reachable values of a split process with recursion + set

resources.title: Sorting theory (merge sort as divide & conquer)

subtopics.name: Merge sort & counting inversions
subtopics.summary: Count pairs i<j with a_i > a_j (inversions) in O(n log n) during merge sort or with a Fenwick tree; parity of inversions decides reachability by swaps. Recognise it whenever crossing pairs, adjacent swaps or "number of pairs with prefix condition" appear.
learn: During merge, when taking from the right half add the number of remaining left elements
Minimum adjacent swaps to sort = number of inversions
A swap changes the inversion parity; a permutation's parity = (n - cycles) mod 2
Generalise: count pairs (i<j) with pre_j - pre_i < t by merge-sorting prefix sums
Bitwise variants: count inversions per bit level on a trie / recursive split

subtopics.name: D&C over the midpoint (static)
subtopics.summary: Answer counting questions over all subarrays by recursing on halves and handling subarrays that cross the midpoint in O(len), or answer offline range queries by splitting at the midpoint (divide-and-conquer static range queries). Recognise it when a property of subarrays is easy to evaluate for those containing a fixed position.
learn: Count crossing subarrays: precompute suffix info of the left half and prefix info of the right half, combine with two pointers or maps
Static range queries: queries crossing mid are answered with precomputed left/right aggregates; others recurse
Split at the maximum and iterate over the smaller side gives O(n log n) (small-to-large)
Total complexity O(n log n) or O(n log^2 n)
Closest pair is a classic instance

subtopics.name: CDQ divide & conquer (offline)
subtopics.summary: CDQ divide and conquer solves offline problems where each update affects later queries (3D partial order, dynamic 2D counting) by recursing on time and letting the left half's updates answer the right half's queries with a sweep + Fenwick tree. Recognise it when a 2D data structure seems necessary but everything is offline.
learn: Sort by first key, recurse on halves, then contribute left-half updates to right-half queries sorted by the second key with a BIT on the third
Complexity O(n log^2 n) with small memory compared to 2D structures
Works for dynamic point-add / rectangle-query by treating time as a dimension
Clear BIT changes by undoing exactly the updates you did
Alternatives: offline 2D BIT, BIT of sorted vectors, wavelet trees

resources.title: CDQ Divide and Conquer
resources.where: Article linked from USACO Guide Platinum 2D Range Queries

subtopics.name: Stack parsing of nested structures
subtopics.summary: Check and repair bracket sequences, match nested structures and simulate nesting with a stack (loops, comments, try/catch blocks). Recognise it from nested input formats or anything with opening/closing tokens.
learn: Balance counter: never negative and ends at 0 for a regular sequence
Stack of positions gives the matching bracket of each closer and the longest regular substring
Multiple bracket types: push the opener, check the type on close
Greedy fixes: count moves/replacements from the minimum prefix balance
Nested multiplications/loops: keep a stack of multipliers and cap values to avoid overflow

subtopics.name: Expression parsing & evaluation
subtopics.summary: Evaluate or transform arithmetic/logical expressions with operator precedence using recursive descent or the shunting-yard (two stacks) algorithm, and build expression trees. Recognise it in problems that give formulas, macro definitions or "insert brackets/operators" tasks.
learn: Recursive descent: expr -> term {(+|-) term}, term -> factor {(*|/) factor}, factor -> number | (expr)
Shunting-yard: operator stack + value stack, pop while top has higher/equal precedence (left-assoc)
Unary minus and right-associative operators need special handling
Build an expression tree to evaluate many assignments or run DP over it
Try all bracket placements only where they matter (around + segments between *)
Parse tokens first (numbers, identifiers, operators) to keep the grammar code simple

subtopics.name: Advanced sqrt heuristics (rebuild, heavy sets, distinct sizes)
subtopics.summary: Beyond plain block decomposition: rebuild a static structure every sqrt(q) updates and handle the buffer by brute force, split sets/vertices into heavy (size > sqrt) and light, and use that a total size n gives only O(sqrt n) distinct sizes. Recognise it when two naive approaches are fast in opposite regimes.
learn: Rebuild every B updates (e.g. multi-source BFS) and answer queries with static data + O(B) buffered updates
Heavy/light sets: at most n/B heavy sets; heavy-heavy and heavy-light pairs are checked differently
Sum of sizes n => at most O(sqrt n) distinct sizes: group equal sizes (binary splitting) for knapsack
Block jump pointers: store where you exit a block and how many steps it takes
Balance B = sqrt(n * cost_a / cost_b); try a few values when constant factors are large
Value thresholds: small values/ratios are enumerated directly, large ones force few candidates (e.g. geometric triples a, ab, ab^2 with b > cube root)

subtopics.name: Timeline simulation & schedules
subtopics.summary: Simulate processes that evolve over time - queues, servers, machines, traffic lights, robots following programs - by jumping from event to event instead of tick by tick, or by finding the period of the process. Recognise it from statements describing who does what at which moment.
learn: Represent the state at event times only; jump time forward to the next event (next arrival, next finish)
Use a queue for FIFO waiting lines and a priority_queue / set of (finish time, id) for servers
If the state space is small, the process is eventually periodic: detect the repeat and skip k mod period steps
Cyclic schedules (lights, repeated programs): work modulo the cycle length and double the string to handle wrap-around
Binary search on the finishing time when tasks can be redistributed (schedule feasibility check)
Be careful with ties: same-time events must follow the statement order
x -> f(x) mod m processes: find the first hit time t0 and the cycle length c (at most m steps each), then solve t0 + k*c for both processes

subtopics.name: Reading problems & constraints
subtopics.summary: Read the whole statement, the constraints and the samples before coding; derive the target complexity from n. Most early wrong answers come from misreading.
learn: n <= 1e5..2e5: O(n log n); n <= 5000: O(n^2); n <= 20: O(2^n * n); n <= 1e18: O(log n) or formula
Re-read the output format and edge cases (n = 1, all equal, negative values)
Work through the samples by hand and invent a small extra test
Check the sum-of-n guarantee over test cases

subtopics.name: Debugging techniques
subtopics.summary: A systematic checklist for wrong answers and runtime errors: overflow, uninitialised data, off-by-one, resetting between test cases, and compiler flags/sanitisers.
learn: Compile with -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG while testing
Check overflow (int vs long long), array bounds, multitest resets
Print intermediate values with a debug macro that is disabled on submit
Re-derive the algorithm on the failing small case by hand

subtopics.name: Stress testing
subtopics.summary: Write a brute-force solution and a random test generator, then compare outputs in a loop to find a small failing test. The fastest way out of "WA on test 2" when you cannot see the bug.
learn: Generator with a seed argument and small parameters (n <= 6) so counterexamples are readable
Brute force that is obviously correct (try all subsets/permutations)
Script: loop { gen > in; sol < in > a; brute < in > b; diff a b || break }
Also stress for time limits with maximum-size tests

subtopics.name: Contest strategy & time management
subtopics.summary: How to allocate time in a 2-hour Codeforces round: read the next problem when stuck, check standings, avoid penalty from careless submissions, and upsolve afterwards.
learn: Solve in order but read one problem ahead; switch if stuck for ~20-30 minutes
Test on samples and an edge case before submitting: each WA costs penalty
Look at the standings to see which problems are being solved
Upsolve 1-2 problems above your level after every contest and read the editorial
